extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; legislators and theorists studying forms of government and citizenship
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's evaluative principles for defining cities, citizenship, virtues of citizens, and the correctness or corruption of government forms. Focuses on criteria for legitimacy, justice, and allocation of political power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen defined by exercising offices
rubrics_metrics.description: "the definition of a citizen is one who exercises certain offices"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats citizenship primarily as a functional/political status (participation in offices and public roles) rather than merely birthplace or legal formality; questions about illegally created citizens should be distinguished from the question of whether they exercise those offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of public managers count as acts of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: "if anything is done by those who have the management of public affairs ... their actions are to be considered as the actions of the state"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing obligations, contracts, or official acts after regime change, treat actions performed by holders of public authority as state actions regardless of regime type (democracy, oligarchy, tyranny); this bears on continuity and responsibility of the city.

rubrics_metrics.name: City identity determined by constitution/government
rubrics_metrics.description: "when we speak of a city as being the same we refer to the government there established"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sameness of a city is grounded in its constitution/mode of government rather than merely location, inhabitants, or walls; a change in the species of government can make the city effectively different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue of a citizen references the state and varies by constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: "the virtue of a citizen has necessarily a reference to the state ... those actions which constitute the virtue of an excellent citizen in one community will not constitute it in another"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What counts as civic excellence depends on the city's constitution and the public roles citizens perform; the virtues that make a 'good man' are not identical with those that make an 'excellent citizen' across all regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the city: living well and making citizens virtuous
rubrics_metrics.description: "a city is a society of people joining together with their families and their children to live agreeably for the sake of having their lives as happy and as independent as possible" and "the first care of him who would found a city ... must be to have his citizens virtuous"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate institutions and distributions of power by whether they promote the good life (eudaimonia) for citizens; a mere alliance for protection or commerce does not fulfill the city's true end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governments are just when they seek the common good
rubrics_metrics.description: "all those governments which have a common good in view are rightly established and strictly just, but those who have in view only the good of the rulers are all founded on wrong principles"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice of a regime is judged by whose interest the supreme power serves — the common good (just) versus the rulers' private good (unjust/tyrannical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of correct and corrupt forms of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct forms: monarchy (one for common good), aristocracy (few/most worthy for common good), polity/state (many for common good). Corruptions: monarchy→tyranny, aristocracy→oligarchy, polity→democracy (as corruption when self-interested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both number of rulers (one/few/many) and whether they govern for common vs private good to classify regimes and diagnose corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy vs democracy distinguished by wealth of rulers (not just number)
rubrics_metrics.description: "an oligarchy and democracy differ ... in the poverty of those who govern in the one, and the riches ... of those who govern in the other"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not define oligarchy/democracy solely by few/many; identify which social class (rich or poor) holds power when labeling a regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who counts as a citizen varies by state and affects civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: "there is a doubt ... whether those only are truly [citizens] who are allowed to share in the government, or whether the mechanics also are to be considered as such?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria for citizenship (e.g., exclusion of mechanics, slaves, or young people) differ by constitutional aims: admitting non-ruling classes alters the homogeneity of civic virtue and the expectations of citizen excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical admission rules reflect demographic needs
rubrics_metrics.description: "there was a law at Thebes that no one could have a share in the government till he had been ten years out of trade ... laws ... are always made in consequence of a scarcity of inhabitants"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for naturalization or extension of citizenship may be pragmatic responses to population needs; when inhabitants are scarce, states relax strict birth/origin requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of honors/power should reflect contribution to the city's end
rubrics_metrics.description: "those who contribute most to this end deserve to have greater power in the city than those who are their equals in family and freedom, but their inferiors in civil virtue"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate political power and honors in proportion to citizens' contribution to promoting the community's happiness and virtue rather than merely on birth or wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme power ought to be lodged with the many (collective competence)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the supreme power ought to be lodged with the many ... when these many are joined together, they may be better qualified ... as a collective body"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues for entrusting significant power to the populace because collective judgment aggregates varied virtues and wisdom; however, this view comes with cautions about ignorance and iniquity of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of political functions: many may elect/censure, few hold top offices
rubrics_metrics.description: "let them then be permitted to vote in the public assemblies and to determine causes ... gave them the power of electing the officers of the state, and also of inquiring into their conduct when they came out of office, and only prevented their being magistrates by themselves"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant the many deliberative and corrective powers (voting, judging, reviewing officials), while reserving certain high magistracies for those of established fortune and worth to balance competence and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of law preferable to rule of an individual
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is wrong to let man have the supreme power and not the law"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws should constrain rulers because individuals are subject to passions; rule according to law is a safeguard against arbitrary government and concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different political roles require different virtues and education
rubrics_metrics.description: "prudence is a necessary qualification for all those who engage in public affairs ... the virtue of the magistrate must be different from the virtue of the citizen"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training of those destined to rule should be specialized (e.g., military or administrative training), since the capacities to command and to obey involve distinct virtues; an accomplished citizen should know both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justice concerns appropriate equality among persons
rubrics_metrics.description: "As to the equality of the things, these they agree in; but their dispute is concerning the equality of the persons ... what is equal appears just, and is so; but not to all; only among those who are equals"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of justice must attend to the relevant basis of equality among persons (e.g., merit, contribution, freedom) rather than applying a single measure across dissimilar persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: A city is defined by shared life, institutions, and customs, not merely place or commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: "a city is not a community of place; nor established for the sake of mutual safety or traffic with each other; but ... a society of people joining together with their families and their children to live agreeably"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether a collection of people constitutes a city, assess shared social institutions (families, marriages, customs, public rituals) and joint pursuit of a good life rather than geographic proximity or trade alone.
